Dear reader,
Creating opportunity requires more than intent –
it is shaped by connection. For the Foundation,
this means bringing together people, knowledge
and resources in ways that open pathways and
reduce barriers.
Wealth inequality is often described in terms of
assets.

Yet what emerges through the Foundation’s
work is that it is fundamentally about access to
education, employment, networks and infrastructure.
Where access is uneven, opportunity cannot flourish.
Effective interventions require more than individual
efforts.

They call for collaboration across sectors,
perspectives and levels of wealth.
The Foundation’s 60th anniversary year was not just
a moment of reflection on the success and learnings
of our work and approach to date. At a time when
division and inequality in the world are becoming
increasingly visible and complex, it was also a year of
action, focused on delivering tangible outcomes.
With ‘The Future of Social Mobility’ Conference in
Chile, co-hosted with COES, the Foundation brought
together leading thinkers and practitioners on social
mobility – enabling new relationships, advancing the
dialogue and laying the groundwork for new solutions
and partnerships.

Elsewhere, collaboration with
partners deepened, with an increasing emphasis on
co-funding with others, recognising that complex
challenges are best addressed together.
The projects featured in this report illustrate the
outcomes of our grant work: supporting young
entrepreneurs in Mexico through access to skills and
mentorship, and enabling young farmers in Zambia
to adopt sustainable practices while connecting
them to markets. Different contexts, but the principles remain the same: creating pathways by linking
those with opportunities to those who can benefit
from them.
The anniversary year also brought renewed engagement through client and employee initiatives, project
partnerships and the Wealth Inequality Initiative,
including the launch of a ‘Knowledge Hub’ and the
‘60 facts on wealth inequality’ series.

By continuing
to open spaces for dialogue and shared learning,
the Foundation reinforces a simple belief: progress
begins with understanding, but is sustained
through connection.
The year also brought changes within the Foundation’s governance. Noel Quinn has assumed the role
of Chairman of the Foundation and in the interview
featured in this report, he shares his perspective on
wealth inequality and the role the Foundation can play
in opening pathways to opportunity. Following her
transition out of the company, Larissa Alghisi Rubner
stepped down from the Board. The Foundation
extends its sincere thanks for her contribution.
Looking ahead, the focus remains on strengthening
these connections – between people, ideas and
resources. Philanthropy has a distinct role to play:
embracing the risk and opportunity that comes with
acting early, bringing together actors who would
not otherwise meet and supporting approaches others
may not yet take on.

Across projects and partner-
ships alike, one thing becomes clear: change does not
happen in isolation. It takes time, trust and collaboration. The Foundation thanks its partners, clients,
employees and peer organisations for shaping this
work together – and for continuing to expand what
is possible.
Yours faithfully,

The Julius Baer Foundation
Wealth inequality is a structural challenge with
far-reaching consequences. It restricts access to
education, healthcare, technology and income
generation – the very things that are needed to
reduce wealth inequality and enable social mobility –
trapping individuals and communities in cycles
of disadvantage. It intersects with many of today’s
most pressing challenges – declining education
and income opportunities, inequality in gender and
in health outcomes, as well as increasing environmental vulnerability. Within these and many
other spheres, unequal starting conditions reinforce
one another over time, narrowing opportunity
across generations.

The knock-on effects are significant and ultimately affect all: Research shows
that high levels of wealth inequality slows economic
growth, weakens household resilience and places
strain on democratic institutions. When large parts
of society lack access to opportunity, trust declines
and social tensions rise.
But the drivers of inequality can also become levers
for change. Addressing wealth inequality requires
dialogue and collaboration across sectors, disciplines
and geographies – and meaningful cooperation
between actors across the wealth spectrum.
The Foundation’s approach
The Foundation works across the wealth divide
to bring together actors to collaborate and expand
opportunity. As the philanthropic arm of a global
wealth manager, the Foundation is uniquely posi-
tioned to bridge perspectives and mobilise actors
from different parts of society.

To put this principle
into practice, the Foundation supports innovative
projects and convenes stakeholders to foster that
collaboration and collective action.
As a funder, the Foundation invests in courageous
ideas and visionary, mostly local, organisations active
in three areas:
• Income generation and enterprise development
• Inclusive education and skills development
• Strengthening community infrastructure
As a convener, the Foundation uses its position
to connect stakeholders who do not typically collaborate: clients, employees, peer foundations, philan-
thropists, and academics. Each contribute expertise,
resources and experience from different angles.
By combining capital, evidence and networks, different
perspectives translate into actionable solutions.
Through curated exchange we co-design, -fund and
-measure pilot ventures for pathways and opport-
unities previously unexplored.

We aim to foster agency
for people of all levels of wealth who want to be part
of the solution.
Our mission: opening pathways
Opportunity is the foundation of prosperous and stable societies.
When talent, effort and ambition can translate into real opportunities, individuals advance, communities thrive and economies
grow.

Yet when access to education, technology, networks and
capital is uneven, this link weakens. Merit no longer determines
outcomes and individual efforts yield diminishing reward. Expanding
access to these resources and strengthening fair starting conditions
is key to rebuilding trust in society and to sustaining prosperity.

Addressing wealth inequality across different spheres
The Julius Baer Foundation supports the United Nations Sustainable Development Agenda and recognises
the importance of collective action in addressing global challenges.

With its focus on reducing wealth
inequality, the Foundation primarily contributes to SDG 10: Reduced Inequalities. As wealth inequality spans
multiple spheres of life, the Foundation, through its partner organisations, also supports progress towards
SDG 1: No Poverty, SDG 4: Quality Education, SDG 5: Gender Equality, SDG 8: Decent Work and Economic
Growth, SDG 11: Sustainable Cities and Communities, and SDG 15: Life on Land.

The Julius Baer Foundation – Interview with the Chairman
In a conversation with the Foundation’s CEO Laura Hemrika,
Noel Quinn, the Chairman of both the Julius Baer Foundation and
the Julius Baer Group, reflects on how opportunity has shaped
his own path, and shares his perspective on wealth inequality and
philanthropy. He highlights the role employment, mentorship
and community infrastructure can play in easing social tensions,
and why philanthropic engagement often provides the crucial spark
for initiatives and solutions that might otherwise never take shape.
“We have been given opportunity”
As one of the leading wealth management firms, addressing wealth inequality
through its Foundation might seem
like a contradiction. Yet to chairman Noel
Quinn, it is a clear opportunity.

Many
of the Bank’s clients do not necessarily
come from wealth. They – himself
included – have created their own wealth
through hard work and dedication, and
thanks to opportunities they were able to
access. Guiding others through that
very journey is a natural linkage between
wealth management and the creation
of opportunities – a connection the Foun-
dation seeks to extend to others.
Wealth is often reduced to assets. More
fundamentally though, it refers to a wealth
of opportunities, to safe living, access
to quality basic services such as education
and healthcare, and a supportive environment and network. Without realising
at the time, Noel now recalls the decisive
moments in his career when people in
his environment were quietly mentoring
him in his development.

Such stewardship
can shape careers and even change the
course of a life.
Access as the make-or-break asset
Wealth inequality is less about the
distribution of assets than about access
While the divide is becoming increasingly
apparent, there are commonalities
between the groups to build upon.
Emerging markets are eager to create
employment in their own markets
and follow the successful road others
have been able to pursue over the
past century through access to energy
and resources.
“I actually think there’s a role for those
that have enjoyed developments in
their markets to try and bring solutions
for the emerging markets.” Access
to water and energy at affordable rates
is critical for sustainable agriculture
and income generation activities. When
access is unavailable, opportunities
across the various spheres of life are
limited. Climate resilience, sustainability
and employability are not isolated
topics but rather interrelated.
Different kinds of capital at work
Philanthropy has a crucial role to play in
this process. It can be that first dollar
toward a blueprint others can follow.

“It’s
having somebody who has good intent,
a vision for how a change can have a
positive impact on people and is willing
to share part of their wealth and be
the founding donation to start a journey.”
The Julius Baer Foundation frequently
invests in very-early-stage projects
to create momentum, leading to more
self-sustaining solutions at a later point.
Philanthropic support might be replaced
through the project’s own momentum,
government support or other economic
institutions. Yet, without that first
donation, energy and work, these initia-
tives would not get off the ground.
Threefold power as a roadmap
The magic happens when connecting
three powerful resources: the work of our
partner organisations on the ground,
the Foundation’s expertise and, often,
clients’ intent.

This triangle of action
is the Foundation’s biggest opportunity.
Noel Quinn
Chairman of the Julius Baer Foundation and Julius
Baer Group, is committed to fostering trust-based
partnerships and inspiring clients, employees, fellow
philanthropists and other foundations to join the
Foundation’s mission.
to education, employment, networks and
even basics such as electricity or food.
Where access is missing, potential remains
unrealised.

What may appear as individual
disadvantage can, at scale, contribute
to wider social divides, growing tensions
and a sense of injustice across communities and societies.
Connecting “those who can create
opportunity with those who need opportunity” is essential to lower tensions
between the different parts of society.
This pioneering type of collaboration
might bring challenges, but to Noel it is
the right way forward. “I don’t think
[this collaboration] should be put off by
tension. I think you try and bring dialogue,
bring connectivity, use networks and
try to remove the tension through collaboration, networking and support. If we
don’t do that, the tension will be even
greater.”
“Connecting those who can
create opportunity with
those who need it is how we
begin to bridge the divide.”
Noel Quinn
Many of the Bank’s clients are genuinely
interested in recycling some of the
benefits they have accumulated to help
others.

Including this group enables
the Foundation to kickstart bigger projects
and more initiatives, a clear ambition
of Noel as chair and current custodian of
the Foundation originally founded by
the Baer family.
Having witnessed the lasting positive
impact on communities that the Foundation, its partner organisations and
clients can achieve together, Noel sees
the next five years as an opportunity
to scale this collaborative model. “Now,
the challenge for us is to do more of that,
start new initiatives, help initiate new
ideas in different markets around the
world [...]. That, for me, is a roadmap that
we can deliver, and hopefully, other
foundations will follow as well.”

Beyond education and skills, today’s reality demands another equally
important asset: the right network.

Even the most dedicated and
talented graduates, entrepreneurs or producers face adversity when
applying for jobs, securing seed funding or building relationships
with distributors without proper connections. The Foundation’s pro-
jects are designed to connect talent with experienced individuals
who have strong networks to open new pathways for growth. The
following four examples highlight the importance of creating value
through personal connection.
Working across the
wealth spectrum
For some of Mexico’s youth, advancing
into decent employment stays out of
reach due to persistent stigmas. Despite
strong credentials, they are unfairly
perceived as less trustworthy and disen-
gaged when stemming from disadvantaged areas with higher violence, unemployment and poor infrastructure. But
this group does not lack perseverance or
skills. They lack access and a professional
network.
The Julius Baer Foundation supports
Forge’s programme “Tu Huella Digital”
(Your Digital Footprint) where stu-
dents from private universities collaborate
with youth that is excluded from valu-
able networks and capital.

Guided by a
team of experts, they co-develop a
creative advertising campaign together.
While the goal of the campaign is to
raise awareness among their peers about
the importance of managing their digital
footprint, the collaboration itself aims at
something even bigger: young people
from all backgrounds across the country
learn to work together as a team, co-gen-
erating ideas, facing challenges, making
decisions and consolidating a project.
It allows them to build bonds of trust and
find common ground before present-
ing their proposal to a jury of experts who
selects a winning idea to be developed
into a high-impact social advertising cam-
paign.
The project offers a safe space for an
enriching peer exchange where individual
backgrounds become irrelevant in the
face of creativity and talent. Michel Lemus
illustrates: “The collaboration let me
create a new network.

It was a great expe-
rience that allowed me to challenge
myself, step out of my comfort zone and
apply all my skills in teamwork to solve
a real-world problem.”
Traditionally, structural barriers have
excluded small-scale seaweed producers
in remote island communities from fair
and direct participation in higher-value
markets.

Despite their earnest efforts,
poor access to information and finance
created dependency on intermedi-
aries to connect their supply with existing
demand.
The Julius Baer Foundation supports
Fundación CODESPA’s project that brings
the small-scale farmers together with
multinational companies to jointly design
a business model that reduces trans-
action costs, increases economic efficiency
and improves profitability for both.
Through in-person field visits between
company managers and producer groups,
they developed a more efficient com-
mercial model. The farmers now produce,
dry and pack seaweed to market speci-
fications, while multinational buyers offer
prices aligned with international standards, eliminating intermediary costs.
The repeated interaction between the two
parties fostered the trust crucial to a
more profitable and sustainable business
relationship. This reliable link motivated
microfinance institutions to recognise sea-
weed farmers as commercially viable,
rather than as high-risk clients.

A specifically designed credit product allows
these communities to expand their oper-
ations and increase their income, while
the microfinanciers benefit from profitable
lending portfolios.
CODESPA’s project is demonstrating
a replicable approach with its inclusive
sourcing model. Seaweed producers
beyond the project’s scope are copying
the framework, creating a cascading
effect that gradually shifts institutional
norms in the local seaweed value chain.

After graduating, girls in rural Zimbabwe

The Julius Baer Foundation supports two
programmes: CAMFED’s new national

with professionals for leadership guidance.
The existing Learner and Transition
Guides Programme supports girls while
in and after graduating secondary school,
creating connections between girls
from rural communities and professionals
and government officials who hold eco-

Guided by a Tran-
sition Guide – a CAMFED graduate
mentoring younger peers – the secondary
school graduates learn about possible
careers, sexual and reproductive health,
and core business and financial skills.
Students are supported to visit tertiary
institutions and professional settings.
For many, this is the first time traveling
beyond their rural villages to visit banks,
hospitals, law firms, magistrates courts,
government departments and vocational
training centres.

The interactions with
professionals from the other end of the
wealth spectrum demystify pathways
usually perceived as inaccessible. As one
student recalls: “Interacting directly with
a doctor helped me understand the aca-
demic path and personal commitment
required to pursue medicine. It motivated
me to focus on chemistry, biology and
mathematics and to remain determined.”
The Zimbabwe Ministry of Primary and
Secondary Education decided to co-deliver
the successful Transition Guide Pro-
gramme in several districts, significantly
amplifying its impact.
Palestinian and Israeli youth often grow

Young

especially non-Israeli youth, also face

The atmosphere was full of energy: 300 international

understanding emerged: We must act together. While
initially reserved, participants found ease in en-
gaging across differences.

Social mobility rarely happens by chance nor
through individual efforts alone. It is shaped by struc-
tures, institutions and the strength of relation-
ships across social groups. When those structures
limit progress, philanthropy can step forward: taking
risks where others cannot, investing patiently and
supporting systemically.

evidence, collaboration and long-term commitment

chains.

insights on this co-funding venture, the benefits and challenges of
such collaborations and the role of the Julius Baer Foundation

The six benefits of co-funding
According to Arunima Singh, co-funding is highly
valuable at two stages: the first is when a project
is ready to scale, and enough data and experience are
available through the work of a first donor to make
investments catalytic. The second is when piloting
high-risk projects where data is still scarce.

In
both cases, co-funding is beneficial for six reasons:
•
Complementary strengths, stronger solutions:
Partners bring distinct expertise, perspectives
and capabilities, strengthening both the design
and delivery of interventions and enabling
more holistic approaches.
•
Fresh perspectives that sharpen thinking:
A second lens introduces constructive challenges
– surfacing blind spots, raising new questions
and ultimately leading to more thoughtful and
robust decision-making.
•
Shared learning and thoughtful capital deployment: Organisations benefit from each other’s
experience, enabling more informed choices and
the ability to commit additional funding as ini-
tiatives mature and risks become clearer over time.
•
Scaling reach and opportunity: By aligning
resources and efforts, organisations can extend
their reach, opening pathways and reducing
barriers for more individuals and communities.
•
Networks that amplify impact: Each partner
contributes access to wider ecosystems and rela-
tionships, creating connections that enhance
collaboration and multiply outcomes over time.
•
From fragmentation to coordinated impact:
Co-funding moves beyond isolated efforts,
fostering more coherent a

nd aligned approaches
that lead to deeper, more sustainable impact.
It also helps foundation teams ensure their own
potential impact is not constrained by what can
often be lean teams.
“The different stakeholders at the table connect dots
for access and visibility, finding and seeing things
that were not visible before.

They have the privilege
of opening doors”, Arunima explains, highlighting
the innovative potential of such partnerships. There
is another advantage to collaborating: “More eyes
to look for red flags is very helpful because it is unfair
to expect organisations to think of everything.”
It takes a village to bring a project to success and by
co-funding, a project gains far more than twice the
funding.
There are challenges to be aware of. Many voices can
“bombard an organisation with too many possible
directions”. Funders’ words carry significant weight
and must be chosen carefully. And vague account-
ability calls for clear roles from the outset.

Still, the
advantages of co-funding outweigh these challenges
as the collaboration between the two foundations
has proved.
Purpose-driven through contextual knowledge
Co-funding the Jojoba for Namibia Trust proved
impactful because Julius Baer Foundation’s contextual knowledge and hands-on approach complemented IMS’s localisation agenda. As a results-driven
organisation, the Julius Baer Foundation invests
in understanding its projects’ contexts and finding
the best funding solutions, customising them to
allow other foundations to join at the scaling stage.
Arunima notes that knowing the ecosystem is
common in venture philanthropy and impact invest-
ment, though less so for traditional foundations.
“I think it’s unique for a foundation of the size of the
Julius Baer Foundation, and it definitely adds value
to organisations like ours, where we can lean into that
information with confidence and trust to amplify
the impact of our investments.”

Joblinge Hamburg, Germany (2019–2025)
Joblinge Munich, Germany (2023–2025)
Joblinge, co-funded with the ‘Julius Bär Stiftung Deutschland’,
supports Germany’s NEET youth (not in education, employment
or training) in overcoming personal and structural barriers
to help them enter the labour market.

The organisation provides
coaching, skills training and direct support in securing appren-
ticeships and formal job placements. During the funding period,
Joblinge Hamburg reached more than 1,800 young people
from underserved backgrounds, with more than 1,200 receiving
direct support. The Julius Baer Foundation’s backing came
at a pivotal moment in the organisation’s growth, and Joblinge is
today firmly established across Germany, with 35 locations
nationwide.

Joblinge’s Munich headquarters additionally devel-
oped and launched an online platform to coordinate the organisation’s extensive volunteer activities.
ISRD Manipur, India (2023–2025)
In Manipur, a landlocked state in India’s Northeast, many girls from
marginalised communities have historically been excluded from
formal education, whether through early dropout or never having
attended school at all.

This project, led by the Institute for
Social Research and Development (ISRD), supported their reinte-
gration into the public education system through four Bridge
Education Centres that provided adapted learning and transition
support. The Centres reached 633 girls, surpassing the original
target, and more than 90% subsequently enrolled in public schools.
ISRD’s holistic approach, engaging families, educators, religious
leaders and local authorities, proved essential to achieving these
results.

Despite the persistent challenges of ongoing ethnic
conflict and severe flooding, the ISRD team was able to continue
their work throughout the project period.
COES, Chile (2022–2025)
The Centre for Social Conflict and Cohesion Studies (COES)
is one of Chile’s leading research institutions on social inequality.
Over three years, six scholars examined upward social mobility
patterns across a broad range of social groups, including execu-
tives, first-generation university graduates, migrants and In-
digenous people, drawing on a survey of 1,528 respondents and
300 in-depth interviews. Among the key outputs are a bilingual
Wealth Inequality Glossary, extensive outreach materials and
the animated video Greater Social Mobility.

The findings were
presented at, and served as the impetus for, the international
conference The Future of Social Mobility in Santiago de Chile in
December 2025, and will be accompanied by a COES publication.
YEFI, Zambia (2025–2028)
The Young Emerging Farmers Initiative (YEFI) is the first organ-
isation in Zambia dedicated exclusively to the needs of young
farmers aged 15 to 35, a generation that is central to the future
of the country’s food systems yet often overlooked by main-
stream agricultural support. YEFI strengthens the resilience of
young small-scale farmers by promoting restorative farming
practices and improving their access to markets. Through its No
Agrochem project, young farmers receive training in agroeco-
logical methods that protect ecosystems, restore degraded soils
and respond to growing demand for high-quality food.

YEFI’s
food-system approach reinforces community networks, connects
producers with buyers and contributes to an enabling policy
environment.
Rainforest Alliance, Colombia & Peru (2025–2028)
The Rainforest Alliance is a global organisation working at the
intersection of environmental sustainability and rural livelihoods.
This project strengthens the organisational, economic and
productive capacities of small-scale coffee and cacao farmers in
the Amazon Basin of Colombia and Peru. Sustainable agriculture
in this biodiversity-rich region supports livelihoods and forest
conversation. With a particular emphasis on including women,
young people and indigenous communities, the initiative promotes
the adoption of climate-smart, regenerative farming practices.
It also improves farmers’ access to credit and supports the instal-
lation of new infrastructure, such as cacao drying and fermen-
tation facilities. Together, these efforts aim to empower previously
underserved groups to increase their yields and meet the stan-
dards required to access more profitable international markets.
